1. Meaning of Fundamental Rights

  • Fundamental Rights are the basic constitutional guarantees protecting liberty, equality, dignity and democratic government.
  • They are contained in Part III of the Constitution.
  • Part III extends from Articles 12 to 35.
  • Fundamental Rights are enforceable through courts.
  • They protect individuals against arbitrary exercise of State power.

They support:

  • Liberty.
  • Equality.
  • Justice.
  • Human dignity.
  • Rule of Law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fundamental Rights → Part III → Articles 12–35

2. Why They Are Called Fundamental

Fundamental Rights are called fundamental because they are:

  • Essential for development of the individual.
  • Necessary for democratic government.
  • Guaranteed by the Constitution.
  • Enforceable through courts.
  • Superior to ordinary legislation.
  • Ordinary laws cannot validly override constitutional Fundamental Rights.

3. Main Objectives of Fundamental Rights

Fundamental Rights seek to:

  • Protect individual liberty.
  • Prevent arbitrary State action.
  • Ensure equality before law.
  • Protect minority interests.
  • Safeguard human dignity.
  • Promote democratic government.
  • Strengthen constitutionalism.

4. Importance in Indian Democracy

Fundamental Rights operate as:

  • Shield against misuse of governmental power.
  • Guarantee of constitutional freedom.
  • Safeguard for minorities.
  • Protection for weaker sections.
  • Foundation of constitutional democracy.
  • Limitation on legislative and executive power.

5. Article 32 — Heart and Soul

  • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the “Heart and Soul of the Constitution.”
  • Article 32 makes Fundamental Rights practically enforceable.
  • Without a constitutional remedy, rights could remain merely declaratory.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 32 → Heart and Soul of Constitution → B.R. Ambedkar

6. Fundamental Rights Are Not Absolute

  • Most Fundamental Rights are subject to constitutional restrictions.

Depending on the right involved, restrictions may relate to:

  • Sovereignty and integrity of India.
  • Security of the State.
  • Friendly relations with foreign States.
  • Public order.
  • Decency.
  • Morality.
  • Contempt of court.
  • Defamation.
  • Incitement to an offence.
  • Restrictions seek to balance liberty with public interest.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Fundamental Rights → Guaranteed but Not Absolute

7. Fundamental Rights and Limited Government

Fundamental Rights promote:

  • Limited government.
  • Constitutional supremacy.
  • Judicial protection.
  • Equality before law.
  • Accountability of State institutions.
  • Rule of Law.
  • Parliamentary democracy operates within these constitutional limitations.

8. Historical Background — Magna Carta, 1215

  • Magna Carta was accepted by King John of England in 1215.
  • It placed important limitations on arbitrary royal authority.
  • It contributed to the principle that even the ruler is subject to law.

Magna Carta → 1215 → Ruler Subject to Law

9. Petition of Right, 1628

The Petition of Right sought protection against:

  • Illegal taxation.
  • Arbitrary imprisonment.
  • Forced military occupation.
  • It contributed to the development of constitutional civil liberties.

10. English Bill of Rights, 1689

The English Bill of Rights strengthened:

  • Parliamentary authority.
  • Civil liberties.
  • Constitutional monarchy.

English Bill of Rights → 1689

11. American Bill of Rights, 1791

  • The first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution are known as the American Bill of Rights.

They protected freedoms relating to:

  • Speech.
  • Religion.
  • Assembly.
  • Fair trial.
  • Personal liberty.
  • American constitutional rights influenced several Indian Fundamental Rights.

12. French Revolution and Rights

The French Revolution of 1789 popularised the principles of:

  • Liberty.
  • Equality.
  • Fraternity.
  • These ideals influenced modern democratic constitutionalism.

  • The Constitution of India Bill, 1895 was among the early Indian constitutional documents demanding civil rights.
  • It reflected growing Indian demands for legally protected liberties.

14. Commonwealth of India Bill, 1925

  • Annie Besant's Commonwealth of India Bill, 1925 contained several civil-liberty provisions.
  • It forms part of the pre-Constitution development of rights demands in India.

15. Nehru Report, 1928

  • The Motilal Nehru Report recommended justiciable Fundamental Rights.

It supported:

  • Equality before law.

Nehru Report → 1928 → Justiciable Rights

16. Karachi Resolution, 1931

  • The Indian National Congress adopted the Karachi Resolution in 1931.

It demanded:

  • Civil liberties.
  • Equality.
  • Labour rights.
  • Religious freedom.
  • Economic justice.
  • It significantly influenced later constitutional thinking.

17. Constituent Assembly and Fundamental Rights

  • The Constituent Assembly examined comparative constitutional systems and democratic principles.
  • Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel chaired the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas.
  • J.B. Kripalani chaired the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee.
  • Their recommendations helped shape Part III.

Advisory Committee → Sardar Patel
Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee → J.B. Kripalani

18. Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948

  • The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1948.

It reinforced global ideals relating to:

  • Equality.
  • Liberty.
  • Human dignity.
  • Freedom.
  • Indian Fundamental Rights were independently framed, but many principles are consistent with the UDHR.

19. Fundamental Rights Became Enforceable

  • Fundamental Rights became enforceable on 26 January 1950.
  • This was the date on which the Constitution came into force.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fundamental Rights Enforceable → 26 January 1950

20. Part III — Constitutional Framework

Part III includes provisions relating to:

  • Definition of State.
  • Judicial review.
  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Constitutional remedies.
  • Parliament's special powers regarding specified rights.
  • Martial law.
  • Armed forces and related services.

21. Original Seven Fundamental Rights

Originally, the Constitution recognised seven broad Fundamental Rights:

  • Right to Equality.
  • Right to Freedom.
  • Right against Exploitation.
  • Right to Freedom of Religion.
  • Cultural and Educational Rights.
  • Right to Constitutional Remedies.
  • Right to Property.

22. Right to Property — Present Position

  • The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 removed the Right to Property from Part III.
  • It ceased to be a Fundamental Right.
  • It now exists under Article 300A as a constitutional legal right.
📌 Must-Memorise

Right to Property → Article 300A
44th Amendment, 1978 → Removed from Fundamental Rights

India presently recognises six categories:

  • Right to Equality.
  • Right to Freedom.
  • Right against Exploitation.
  • Right to Freedom of Religion.
  • Cultural and Educational Rights.
  • Right to Constitutional Remedies.

25. Rights Available to Persons

Important rights available to persons generally include:

  • Article 14.
  • Article 20.
  • Article 21.
  • Article 21A.
  • Article 22.
  • Articles 25–28 subject to their wording.
  • Foreigners may therefore enjoy several Fundamental Rights.

26. Rights Available Only to Citizens

Important citizen-oriented rights include:

  • Article 15.
  • Article 16.
  • Article 19.
  • Article 29.
  • Article 30 protects religious and linguistic minorities.

27. Rights Operating against Private Persons

Fundamental Rights generally operate against the State.

However, important provisions such as:

  • Article 17.
  • Article 23.
  • Article 24

also impose obligations in private relationships.

📌 Must-Memorise

Private Enforcement → Articles 17, 23, 24

28. Importance of Article 12

  • Article 12 defines “State” for purposes of Part III.
  • Fundamental Rights are primarily enforceable against the State.
  • Therefore, Article 12 acts as the gateway to constitutional accountability.
📌 Gateway Question

Is the action attributable to “State” under Article 12?

29. Article 12 — Authorities Included

For Part III, “State” includes:

  • Government of India.
  • Parliament of India.
  • Government of each State.
  • Legislature of each State.
  • Local authorities.
  • Other authorities within the territory of India.
  • Other authorities under the control of the Government of India.

30. Government of India under Article 12

The Union Executive includes:

  • President.
  • Prime Minister.
  • Union Council of Ministers.
  • Ministries.
  • Central government departments.
  • Executive actions of the Union must comply with Fundamental Rights.

31. Parliament under Article 12

  • Parliament forms part of “State.”

Parliament constitutionally consists of:

  • President.
  • Rajya Sabha.
  • Lok Sabha.
  • Parliamentary laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights may be constitutionally challenged.

32. State Government and Legislature under Article 12

State Government includes:

  • Governor.
  • Chief Minister.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • State departments.
  • Administrative authorities.

State Legislature includes:

  • Legislative Assembly.
  • Legislative Council where it exists.

33. Local Authorities under Article 12

Examples include:

  • Municipal Corporations.
  • Municipalities.
  • Panchayats.
  • Zila Parishads.
  • District Boards.
  • Port Trusts.
  • Improvement Trusts.
  • Local authorities are therefore subject to Part III constitutional limitations.

34. “Other Authorities”

The expression “other authorities” may include bodies such as:

  • Statutory corporations.
  • Public Sector Undertakings.
  • Government companies.
  • Development authorities.
  • Statutory universities.
  • Electricity Boards.
  • Public financial institutions.
  • Regulatory bodies.
  • Government-controlled societies.
  • Actual inclusion depends on constitutional tests developed by courts.

35. Private Bodies and Article 12

  • Private companies, clubs and associations do not automatically become “State.”
  • The organisation's name or legal form alone is not decisive.
  • A private body performing public duties may still become subject to remedies under Article 226 in appropriate circumstances.
  • Specific Fundamental Rights may also operate directly against private persons.

36. Rajasthan State Electricity Board v. Mohan Lal, 1967

  • This was an important early case interpreting “other authorities.”
  • The Supreme Court held that statutory authorities created by law may fall within Article 12.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajasthan Electricity Board Case → 1967 → Other Authorities

37. Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagatram, 1975

The Supreme Court treated statutory corporations such as:

  • ONGC.
  • LIC.
  • IFCI

as “State” because of their statutory public character.

38. R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority, 1979

  • The Supreme Court developed the instrumentality or agency approach.
  • Substantial governmental control may indicate that a body is “State.”
📌 Must-Memorise

R.D. Shetty → 1979 → Instrumentality/Agency Test

39. Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib, 1981

  • The legal form of an organisation is not decisive.
  • Even a registered society may fall under Article 12 if it operates as an instrumentality or agency of government.

Relevant indicators include:

  • Financial assistance.
  • Administrative control.
  • Functional control.
  • Government domination.
  • Public importance.

40. Zee Telefilms v. Union of India, 2005

  • The Supreme Court held that BCCI was not “State” under Article 12 because it was not substantially government-controlled.
  • The Court nevertheless recognised that remedies may sometimes lie under Article 226 against private bodies performing public duties.
📌 Must-Memorise

Zee Telefilms → 2005 → BCCI Not State under Article 12

41. Importance of Article 13

  • Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void to the extent of inconsistency.

It reinforces:

  • Constitutional supremacy.
  • Judicial review.
  • Limitation on legislative power.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 13 → Laws Violating Fundamental Rights → Void to Extent of Inconsistency

42. Article 13(1)

  • Article 13(1) deals with pre-Constitution laws.
  • Laws in force before 26 January 1950 become void to the extent they conflict with Fundamental Rights.
  • The inconsistent portion becomes unenforceable.
  • This provision is linked to the Doctrine of Eclipse.

43. Article 13(2)

  • The State shall not make laws taking away or abridging Fundamental Rights.
  • Any such law is void to the extent of the violation.
  • This applies to future legislation by Parliament and State Legislatures.

44. Article 13(3) — Meaning of Law

For Article 13, “law” includes:

  • Acts.
  • Ordinances.
  • Rules.
  • Regulations.
  • Notifications.
  • Bye-laws.
  • Customs having force of law.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

Article 13 “Law” → Wider than Acts Alone

45. Article 13(4)

  • Article 13(4) was inserted by the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971.
  • It declares that constitutional amendments under Article 368 are not “law” for purposes of Article 13.
  • Constitutional amendments remain subject to the Basic Structure Doctrine.
📌 Must-Memorise

24th Amendment → Article 13(4)

46. Meaning of “Void to the Extent”

  • Article 13 does not always invalidate an entire law.
  • Only the unconstitutional portion may become void.
  • The remaining valid portion can survive if separable.
  • This forms the basis of the Doctrine of Severability.

47. Meaning of Judicial Review

  • Judicial review allows constitutional courts to examine whether laws and executive actions conform to the Constitution.
  • Unconstitutional laws may be struck down.
  • It preserves constitutional supremacy and limited government.

48. Constitutional Basis of Judicial Review

Judicial review draws support from provisions including:

  • Article 13.
  • Article 32.
  • Article 131.
  • Article 136.
  • Article 226.
  • Article 227.
  • Article 246.
  • Article 254.
📌 Must-Memorise

Judicial Review → Not Based on One Article Alone

49. What Can Be Reviewed

Courts may review:

  • Parliamentary laws.
  • State laws.
  • Ordinances.
  • Rules.
  • Regulations.
  • Notifications.
  • Executive orders.
  • Administrative decisions.
  • Delegated legislation.

50. Judicial Review vs Judicial Supremacy

  • Judicial review does not mean Judiciary is superior to Constitution or all other organs.
  • Parliament makes laws.
  • Executive implements laws.
  • Judiciary examines constitutional validity.
  • Constitutional supremacy remains the controlling principle.

51. State of Madras v. V.G. Row, 1952

  • The Supreme Court emphasised judicial examination of the reasonableness of restrictions on Fundamental Rights.
  • The case strengthened judicial review under Article 19.

52. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973

  • Parliament may amend the Constitution.
  • It cannot destroy the Basic Structure.
  • Judicial review was recognised as an important Basic Structure feature.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kesavananda Bharati → 1973 → Basic Structure

53. Minerva Mills v. Union of India, 1980

  • The Court reaffirmed limited amending power.
  • Judicial review was reaffirmed as part of the Basic Structure.
  • Balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles was also protected.

54. L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997

  • Judicial review by the Supreme Court and High Courts cannot be excluded by tribunal legislation.
  • Constitutional judicial review forms part of the Basic Structure.

55. Doctrine of Severability

  • If only part of a law is unconstitutional, the invalid part may be removed while the valid remainder survives.
  • The doctrine arises from the words “to the extent of” in Article 13.
📌 Must-Memorise

Severability → Invalid Part Removed; Valid Part Survives

56. Conditions for Severability

The doctrine applies where:

  • Valid and invalid provisions are separable.
  • Remaining provisions can operate independently.
  • Legislative purpose can still be achieved.
  • If the invalid provision is inseparable from the whole statute, the entire law may fail.

57. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala v. Union of India, 1957

  • The Supreme Court elaborated the Doctrine of Severability.
  • Valid portions should be preserved if capable of independent operation.
📌 Must-Memorise

R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala → 1957 → Severability

58. Doctrine of Eclipse

  • The Doctrine of Eclipse primarily applies to pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
  • Such laws are not treated as completely dead.
  • They become unenforceable to the extent of inconsistency.
  • They remain under a constitutional “eclipse.”

59. Effect of Eclipse

A pre-Constitution law:

  • Continues to exist.
  • Is not necessarily repealed.
  • Becomes unenforceable against persons protected by the conflicting Fundamental Right.
  • May revive if the constitutional inconsistency is removed.

60. Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 1955

  • This is the leading case on the Doctrine of Eclipse.
  • A pre-Constitution law became inoperative due to inconsistency with Fundamental Rights.
  • When the constitutional obstacle was later removed, the law revived.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhikaji Narain Dhakras → 1955 → Eclipse

61. Doctrine of Waiver

  • Waiver means voluntary surrender of a legal right.
  • Fundamental Rights cannot ordinarily be waived.
  • These rights protect both individuals and the broader constitutional order.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fundamental Rights → Cannot Ordinarily Be Waived

62. Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income Tax, 1959

  • The Supreme Court held that an individual cannot waive Fundamental Rights.
  • Government cannot validate a constitutional violation merely by obtaining private consent.
📌 Must-Memorise

Basheshar Nath → 1959 → Waiver

63. Right to Equality — Overview

The Right to Equality includes:

  • Article 14 → Equality before law and equal protection.
  • Article 15 → Prohibition of discrimination.
  • Article 16 → Equality in public employment.
  • Article 17 → Abolition of untouchability.
  • Article 18 → Abolition of titles.

64. Article 14 — Equality before Law

  • Equality before law means no person enjoys arbitrary privilege before ordinary law.
  • Every person is equally subject to law.
  • This is associated with the British Rule of Law tradition of A.V. Dicey.
  • It is usually described as a negative concept.
📌 Must-Memorise

Equality Before Law → British Origin → Negative Concept

65. Article 14 — Equal Protection of Laws

  • Equal protection requires similar treatment of persons similarly situated.
  • It allows reasonable classification.
  • It is commonly associated with American constitutional influence.
  • It is described as a positive concept.
📌 Must-Memorise

Equal Protection → American Origin → Positive Concept

66. Reasonable Classification

A constitutional classification must satisfy:

  • Intelligible Differentia.
  • Rational Nexus.
  • Intelligible Differentia → Clear basis distinguishing one group from another.
  • Rational Nexus → The classification must relate reasonably to the objective of the law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Reasonable Classification → Intelligible Differentia + Rational Nexus

67. Article 14 — What It Prohibits and Permits

Article 14 prohibits:

  • Arbitrary State action.
  • Class legislation.
  • Unreasonable discrimination.

Article 14 permits:

  • Reasonable classification.
  • Protective discrimination.
  • Affirmative action.
  • Welfare legislation.
  • Constitutionally valid special provisions.

68. Article 15 — Prohibition of Discrimination

  • Article 15 protects citizens against specified discrimination.

The State shall not discriminate only on grounds of:

  • Religion.
  • Race.
  • Caste.
  • Sex.
  • Place of birth.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 15 Grounds → Religion + Race + Caste + Sex + Place of Birth

69. Article 15 and Public Places

Citizens cannot be denied access merely on prohibited grounds to places such as:

  • Shops.
  • Hotels.
  • Restaurants.
  • Public wells.
  • Roads.
  • Tanks.
  • Bathing ghats.
  • Places of public resort.

70. Special Provisions Permitted under Article 15

Article 15 allows special provisions for:

  • Women.
  • Children.
  • Socially and Educationally Backward Classes.
  • Scheduled Castes.
  • Scheduled Tribes.
  • Economically Weaker Sections.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Article 15 → Prohibits Discrimination + Permits Protective Measures

71. Article 15 — Key Amendments

  • 93rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2005 → Enabled reservation in educational institutions subject to constitutional limitations, excluding Article 30 minority educational institutions.
  • 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 → Introduced EWS reservation provisions.
📌 Must-Memorise

93rd → Article 15(5)
103rd → Article 15(6)

72. Article 16 — Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment

  • Article 16 applies to public employment under the State.
  • It guarantees equality of opportunity to eligible citizens.

Discrimination is prohibited on grounds including:

  • Religion.
  • Race.
  • Caste.
  • Sex.
  • Descent.
  • Place of birth.
  • Residence.

73. Exceptions under Article 16

The Constitution permits:

  • Residence requirements where Parliament prescribes them.
  • Reservation for backward classes.
  • Reservation for SCs.
  • Reservation for STs.
  • Reservation for EWS.
  • Reservation in promotion for SC/ST subject to constitutional requirements.
  • Religious qualifications for certain religious institutions.

74. Reservation and Substantive Equality

  • Reservation seeks adequate representation and social justice.
  • It is an instrument for substantive equality.
  • Constitutional equality does not always require identical treatment.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Reservation → Substantive Equality

75. Article 17 — Abolition of Untouchability

  • Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
  • Its practice in any form is prohibited.
  • Enforcement of disability arising from untouchability is punishable by law.
  • Article 17 operates against both State and private individuals.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 17 → Abolition of Untouchability

76. Laws Supporting Article 17

Important laws include:

  • Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.
  • It was originally called the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955.
  • Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

77. Article 18 — Abolition of Titles

  • Article 18 abolishes titles creating artificial social distinctions.

The State may confer:

  • Military distinctions.
  • Academic distinctions.
  • Indian citizens cannot accept titles from foreign States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 18 → Abolition of Titles

78. National Awards and Article 18

Awards such as:

  • Bharat Ratna.
  • Padma Vibhushan.
  • Padma Bhushan.
  • Padma Shri

are not prohibited titles under Article 18.

  • They cannot be used as hereditary prefixes or suffixes creating social rank.

79. Permissible Distinctions

Military distinctions include examples such as:

  • Param Vir Chakra.
  • Ashoka Chakra.
  • Maha Vir Chakra.
  • Vir Chakra.

Academic distinctions include:

  • Degrees.
  • Academic qualifications.

80. Article 19 — Six Freedoms

Article 19 presently guarantees six freedoms to citizens:

  • Speech and expression.
  • Peaceful assembly without arms.
  • Association, union or cooperative society.
  • Movement throughout India.
  • Residence and settlement.
  • Profession, occupation, trade or business.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 19 → Six Freedoms → Citizens Only

81. Original Seventh Freedom

  • Article 19 originally contained seven freedoms.
  • The Right to Property under Article 19(1)(f) was removed by the 44th Amendment, 1978.

82. Article 19(1)(a) — Speech and Expression

Freedom of speech and expression includes:

  • Expressing opinions.
  • Sharing information.
  • Criticising government.
  • Publishing books and newspapers.
  • Artistic expression.
  • Academic discussion.
  • Political criticism.
  • Digital communication.

83. Freedom of Press

  • Freedom of the press is not separately written as an independent Article.
  • It is judicially recognised within Article 19(1)(a).
📌 Must-Memorise

Freedom of Press → Article 19(1)(a)

84. Grounds of Restriction under Article 19(2)

Speech may be reasonably restricted on grounds of:

  • Sovereignty and integrity of India.
  • Security of the State.
  • Friendly relations with foreign States.
  • Public order.
  • Decency.
  • Morality.
  • Contempt of court.
  • Defamation.
  • Incitement to an offence.

85. Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras, 1950

  • The Supreme Court recognised freedom of speech as foundational to democracy.
  • It is an important early Article 19 case.

86. Bennett Coleman v. Union of India, 1973

  • The Supreme Court affirmed freedom of the press under Article 19(1)(a).

87. Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, 2015

  • The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act.
  • The case is a major modern freedom-of-speech decision.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shreya Singhal → 2015 → Section 66A Struck Down

88. Article 19(1)(b) — Peaceful Assembly

  • Citizens may assemble peacefully and without arms.

Protected activities may include:

  • Public meetings.
  • Peaceful demonstrations.
  • Rallies.
  • Violent or armed gatherings are not protected.

Restrictions may relate to:

  • Sovereignty and integrity of India.
  • Public order.

89. Article 19(1)(c) — Associations

Citizens may form:

  • Associations.
  • Unions.
  • Cooperative societies.
  • Trade unions.
  • Political parties.
  • Professional bodies.
  • Cultural organisations.
  • The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011 added “co-operative societies” to Article 19(1)(c).
📌 Must-Memorise

97th Amendment → Cooperative Societies in Article 19(1)(c)

90. Restrictions on Associations

Restrictions may be imposed in the interests of:

  • Sovereignty and integrity of India.
  • Public order.
  • Morality.

91. Article 19(1)(d) — Movement

  • Citizens may move freely throughout India.

Restrictions may be imposed:

  • In general public interest.
  • For protection of Scheduled Tribe interests.
  • In specified protected or sensitive areas.

92. Article 19(1)(e) — Residence

  • Citizens may reside and settle in any part of India.

This supports:

  • Single citizenship.
  • Internal mobility.
  • National integration.
  • Restrictions may exist in public interest or for protection of Scheduled Tribes.

93. Article 19(1)(g) — Profession and Business

Citizens may:

  • Practise any profession.
  • Carry on any occupation.
  • Conduct trade.
  • Conduct business.

The State may impose:

  • Reasonable public-interest restrictions.
  • Professional qualifications.
  • Technical qualifications.
  • State monopolies in specified sectors.

94. Reasonableness of Restrictions

Courts examine whether restrictions are:

  • Fair.
  • Non-arbitrary.
  • Reasonably connected to constitutional objectives.
  • Proportionate to the purpose.

95. Article 20 — Protection in Criminal Cases

Article 20 protects every person through three safeguards:

  • Ex-post facto protection.
  • Double jeopardy.
  • Protection against self-incrimination.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 20 → 3 Criminal-Law Protections

96. Article 20(1) — Ex-Post Facto Law

  • No person can be convicted for an act that was not an offence when committed.
  • No greater punishment can be imposed than the punishment applicable when the offence was committed.
  • A beneficial criminal law reducing punishment may operate retrospectively.

97. Article 20(2) — Double Jeopardy

  • No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.

The maxim associated with the principle is:

  • Nemo debet bis vexari.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 20(2) → Double Jeopardy

98. Article 20(3) — Self-Incrimination

  • No accused person can be compelled to be a witness against himself.
  • It protects against forced testimonial confession.
  • It applies to a person accused of an offence.

It does not prevent lawful collection of physical evidence such as:

  • Fingerprints.
  • Handwriting.
  • DNA.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 20(3) → Self-Incrimination

99. Article 21 — Life and Personal Liberty

  • Article 21 provides that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
  • It protects citizens and foreigners, subject to constitutional exceptions.
  • Article 21 has received expansive judicial interpretation.

100. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, 1978

  • Maneka Gandhi transformed Article 21 jurisprudence.

Procedure affecting liberty must be:

  • Fair.
  • Just.
  • Reasonable.

104. Article 22 — Arrest and Detention

Article 22 deals with:

  • Ordinary arrest.
  • Preventive detention.
  • It protects citizens and foreigners subject to constitutional exceptions such as enemy aliens and preventive-detention provisions.

105. Safeguards on Ordinary Arrest

A person arrested is entitled to:

  • Information on grounds of arrest.
  • Legal practitioner of choice.
  • Production before nearest Magistrate within 24 hours.
  • Travel time excluded.
  • No detention beyond 24 hours without Magistrate's authority.

106. Preventive Detention

  • Preventive detention seeks to prevent anticipated harmful activity.
  • It is different from punishment for a past offence.

It may relate to concerns such as:

  • National security.
  • Public order.
  • Defence.
  • Foreign affairs.
  • Essential public interests.

107. Safeguards in Preventive Detention

Safeguards include:

  • Communication of grounds subject to exceptions.
  • Opportunity to make representation.
  • Review by an Advisory Board within the prescribed framework.

108. Article 23 — Trafficking and Forced Labour

Article 23 prohibits:

  • Human trafficking.
  • Begar.
  • Forced labour.
  • Similar forms of compulsory labour.
  • It applies to citizens and foreigners.
  • It also binds private persons.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 23 → Trafficking + Begar + Forced Labour

109. Human Trafficking under Article 23

Trafficking may include:

  • Buying and selling human beings.
  • Forced prostitution.
  • Sexual exploitation.
  • Forced marriage.
  • Organ trafficking.
  • Forced domestic labour.
  • Child trafficking.
  • Recruitment for exploitation.

110. Begar

  • Begar means compulsory labour without payment.
  • Article 23 abolishes this exploitative practice.

111. Forced Labour and Minimum Wages

  • Forced labour is not limited to physical force.
  • Economic compulsion can also amount to forced labour.
  • Payment below statutory minimum wages may fall within Article 23 according to judicial interpretation.

112. Compulsory Public Service

  • Article 23 permits compulsory service for public purposes.

Such service cannot discriminate only on grounds such as:

  • Religion.
  • Race.
  • Caste.
  • Class.

113. Laws Supporting Article 23

Examples include:

  • Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976.
  • Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956.
  • Child and Adolescent Labour legislation.
  • Criminal-law provisions dealing with trafficking and exploitation.

114. People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India, 1982

  • Also known as the Asiad Workers Case.
  • Payment below statutory minimum wage may amount to forced labour.
  • Economic compulsion can come within Article 23.
📌 Must-Memorise

PUDR / Asiad Workers → 1982 → Forced Labour + Minimum Wage

115. Article 24 — Child Labour

Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in:

  • Factories.
  • Mines.
  • Hazardous employment.
  • It operates against both State and private employers.

  • Article 24 protects children from hazardous labour.
  • Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14.

  • The Child and Adolescent Labour law generally prohibits employment of children below 14 subject to statutory exceptions.
  • Adolescents aged 14–18 are prohibited from hazardous occupations and processes.

118. M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu, 1996

  • The Supreme Court dealt with child labour.

  • Compensation.

119. Secular Framework

  • India is a secular Republic.
  • Articles 25–28 protect religious freedom.

These provisions combine:

  • Freedom of conscience.
  • Religious practice.
  • Institutional autonomy.
  • State neutrality.
  • Permissible social reform.

120. Article 25 — Freedom of Religion

Article 25 guarantees every person:

  • Freedom of conscience.
  • Freedom to profess religion.
  • Freedom to practise religion.
  • Freedom to propagate religion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 25 → Conscience + Profess + Practise + Propagate

121. Limits under Article 25

Article 25 is subject to:

  • Public order.
  • Morality.
  • Health.
  • Other Fundamental Rights.
  • The State may regulate secular activities associated with religion.
  • The State may undertake social welfare and reform.

122. Conscience, Profession, Practice and Propagation

  • Conscience → Inner freedom of belief or non-belief.
  • Profession → Open declaration of faith.
  • Practice → Religious rituals and observances.
  • Propagation → Spreading or explaining religious beliefs.

123. Propagation and Conversion

Propagation does not create a Fundamental Right to convert another person by:

  • Force.
  • Fraud.
  • Inducement.

124. Rev. Stainislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 1977

  • The Supreme Court upheld the distinction between propagation and forced or fraudulent conversion.
  • States may regulate unlawful conversion practices.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rev. Stainislaus → 1977 → Propagation ≠ Forced Conversion

125. Article 26 — Religious Denominations

Every religious denomination or section thereof may, subject to public order, morality and health:

  • Establish religious or charitable institutions.
  • Manage religious affairs.
  • Own and acquire property.
  • Administer property according to law.

126. Religious Matters vs Secular Administration

  • Religious autonomy does not prevent State regulation of secular administration.

The State may regulate:

  • Finance.
  • Property management.
  • Public order.
  • Social reform.
  • Secular activities associated with religion.

127. Essential Religious Practices Doctrine

  • Courts developed the Essential Religious Practices Doctrine.
  • Practices considered essential to religion may receive constitutional protection.
  • Secular or administrative matters may be regulated.

128. Shirur Mutt Case, 1954

  • Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar is commonly called the Shirur Mutt Case.
  • It recognised denominational autonomy in essential religious matters.
  • It also recognised State regulation of secular administration.
  • It laid the foundation for the Essential Religious Practices doctrine.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shirur Mutt → 1954 → Articles 25–26

129. Article 27 — Religious Taxation

  • No person can be compelled to pay taxes specifically appropriated for promoting or maintaining a particular religion or denomination.
  • Article 27 supports State neutrality.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 27 → No Tax for Promotion of Particular Religion

130. Tax vs Regulatory Fee

  • A tax specifically appropriated for promotion of one religion is constitutionally restricted.
  • Regulatory fees for secular administrative purposes may be permissible.

131. Article 28 — Religious Instruction

Article 28 regulates religious instruction in educational institutions.

132. Wholly State-Funded Institutions

  • No religious instruction may be provided in educational institutions wholly maintained out of State funds.

133. Trust or Endowment Exception

  • If an institution is administered by the State but established under an endowment or trust requiring religious instruction, such instruction may continue.

134. State-Recognised or State-Aided Institutions

  • No person attending a State-recognised or State-aided institution may be compelled to participate in religious instruction or worship without consent.
  • For minors, guardian consent is relevant.

135. Articles 25–28 — Mapping

  • Article 25 → Individual religious freedom.
  • Article 26 → Religious denominations.
  • Article 27 → Religious taxation.
  • Article 28 → Religious instruction.

136. Article 29 — Cultural Protection

  • Article 29 protects language, script and culture of sections of citizens.
  • It is not confined only to minorities.
  • Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture may seek protection.

A section of citizens may conserve:

  • Language.
  • Script.
  • Culture.

No citizen shall be denied admission to State-maintained or State-aided educational institutions only on grounds of:

  • Race.

  • Language.

  • Article 30 gives religious and linguistic minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

140. Minority Status

Article 30 protects:

  • Religious minorities.
  • Linguistic minorities.

141. Rights under Article 30

Minorities may:

  • Establish institutions.
  • Administer institutions.
  • Appoint management.
  • Preserve educational objectives.
  • Use education to maintain cultural identity.

142. State Aid and Article 30

  • The State cannot discriminate in granting aid merely because an educational institution is minority-managed.
  • Receiving aid does not automatically extinguish Article 30 protection.

143. Permissible Regulation of Minority Institutions

The State may regulate:

  • Academic standards.
  • Public health.
  • Sanitation.
  • Teacher qualifications.
  • Educational excellence.
  • Regulation cannot destroy the minority character of the institution.

144. St. Xavier's College v. State of Gujarat, 1974

  • The Supreme Court recognised substantial administrative autonomy of minority educational institutions.
  • Reasonable regulation for educational standards remains permissible.

145. T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka, 2002

An Eleven-Judge Bench clarified:

  • Meaning of minority institutions.
  • Administrative rights.
  • Government regulation.
  • Balance between autonomy and educational standards.

  • Protects language, script and culture.

147. Article 32 — Nature

  • Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
  • Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.
  • It converts constitutional rights into enforceable guarantees.

148. Writs under Article 32

The Supreme Court may issue:

  • Habeas Corpus.
  • Mandamus.
  • Prohibition.
  • Certiorari.
  • Quo Warranto.

149. Who May Approach Supreme Court

  • A person whose Fundamental Rights are violated may approach the Supreme Court.

Procedural rules have been relaxed in appropriate cases through:

  • Public Interest Litigation.
  • Epistolary jurisdiction.

150. Limits of Article 32

  • Article 32 is specifically for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

It is not ordinarily used merely for:

  • Contractual disputes.
  • Service matters.
  • Ordinary property disputes.
  • Purely civil rights
    unless a Fundamental Right is involved.

151. Article 32 vs Article 226

Article 32:

  • Supreme Court.
  • Enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
  • Itself a Fundamental Right.

Article 226:

  • High Courts.
  • Fundamental Rights and other legal rights.
  • Wider remedial scope.
  • Subject to High Court territorial jurisdiction.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 32 → Supreme Court
Article 226 → High Courts

  • The Supreme Court expanded access to justice through PIL in bonded-labour and dignity cases.

  • L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997 affirmed judicial review by constitutional courts as part of the Basic Structure.

The purpose is to ensure:

  • Discipline.
  • Proper discharge of duties.
  • National security.

  • The Constitution does not expressly define martial law.

  • Fundamental Rights are subject to constitutionally authorised limitations.

  • Authorised by law.
  • Directed to a legitimate purpose.
  • Fair.
  • Non-arbitrary.
  • Proportionate.

  • Justiciable.
  • Enforceable by courts.
  • Protect individual liberty.
  • Civil and political focus.

DPSP:

  • Non-justiciable.
  • Not directly enforceable.
  • Guide governance.
  • Social and economic welfare focus.

  • Part III promotes political democracy.
  • Part IV seeks social and economic democracy.
  • The Constitution aims to achieve both.
